issues.legal_issue: Different treatment of religious trusts associated with different religious communities is constitutionally permissible when the classification rests on relevant differences and is rationally related to the legislation’s purpose.
material_facts: The challenged legislation covered Hindu and Jain religious trusts but excluded Sikh religious trusts, and provided distinct arrangements for the two main Jain branches.
The religious communities differed in beliefs, practices, and the organization of their religious trusts; the needs of Hindu and Jain trusts in administration were not the same.
The legislation was intended to improve the administration of religious trusts and protect and preserve trust property.
issues.conclusion: The classification did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 forbids class legislation but permits reasonable classification where it is based on an intelligible differentia distinguishing those included from those excluded and that differentia has a rational relation to the statute’s object. The Court relied on Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, [1959] S.C.R. 279, and stated that constitutionality is presumed and the challenger bears the burden of showing a clear infringement.

predicates.challenge_to_religious_trust_regulation: The litigants challenged a law governing the administration of religious trusts.
predicates.religious_groups_differ_in_trust_organiz: The religious communities whose trusts were treated differently had distinct practices or organizational arrangements for their trusts.
predicates.classification_tracks_relevant_differenc: The legislature grouped or separated trusts according to differences relevant to their administration.
predicates.classification_advances_regulatory_purpo: The classification related to the legislation’s aim of improving trust administration and protecting trust property.

issues.definition: When a challenge to religious-trust regulation concerns groups with different trust arrangements, and the classification reflects those differences and advances the regulatory purpose, the classification is constitutionally permissible.

issues.legal_issue: Restrictions on a religious-trust manager’s control of trust property are permissible when they reasonably serve proper administration and protection of the trust and include safeguards against misuse of the regulatory powers.
material_facts: The legislation gave the Board supervisory and administrative powers, including powers relating to budgets, inspection, directions to trustees, schemes, and removal of trustees in specified circumstances.
The legislation directed that trusts be properly supervised and that their income be applied to their objects and purposes.

The Board’s powers were subject to safeguards, including consistency with the founder’s ascertainable wishes and the trust’s governing law, and opportunities to seek judicial review of certain decisions.
Before the legislation, section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure provided a court-based procedure to enforce duties relating to public charitable or religious trusts.
issues.conclusion: The restrictions were reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public and did not violate the right to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f), subject to Article 19(5), allowed reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public. The Court considered the purpose of the Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950, and its safeguards, and relied on Angurbala Mullick v. Debabrata Mullick, [1951] S.C.R. 1125, concerning a shebait’s mixed duties and beneficial interest. It distinguished The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, [1954] S.C.R. 1005, and Mahant Shri Jagannath Ramanuj Das v. The State of Orissa, [1954] S.C.R. 1046, where different statutory provisions were held unreasonable.

predicates.challenge_to_religious_trust_regulation: The litigants challenged a law regulating the management of religious trusts.
predicates.regulation_limits_trustee_control: The law gave a public regulatory body powers that restricted a trustee’s control over trust affairs or property.
predicates.limits_serve_trust_administration_and_pr: The restrictions were directed to proper administration of the trust and protection or preservation of its property.
predicates.regulatory_powers_have_effective_safegua: The law limited the regulator’s powers and provided safeguards or review against improper exercise.

issues.definition: Where a trust-regulation challenge concerns limits on trustee control that serve trust administration and preservation and are subject to effective safeguards, those property restrictions are reasonable in the general public interest.

issues.legal_issue: Regulatory supervision of a religious trust does not violate religious freedom or a denomination’s right to manage religious affairs when it preserves religious practices and directs trust property to the purposes established by the founder or usage.
material_facts: The Board could alter or modify a trust budget and give directions to a trustee.

Budget changes could not be inconsistent with the founder’s ascertainable wishes or the governing law, and directions had to be for proper administration in accordance with the governing law and those wishes.
The legislation was directed to administration of the trusts and protection of trust property, not to changing religious practices or diverting trust funds to different purposes.
The appellants identified no provision that interfered with religious practices or with the right to establish and maintain religious institutions.
issues.conclusion: The legislation did not contravene the constitutional protections for religious freedom and the management of religious affairs.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 25 and 26 protect religious belief and practice and a denomination’s management of its affairs in matters of religion. The Court relied on The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, [1954] S.C.R. 1005, including its recognition that religious freedom extends to religious practices; Sri Venkataramana Devaru v. The State of Mysore, [1958] S.C.R. 895; and Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. The State of Bombay, [1954] S.C.R. 1055, concerning the use of religious trust property for the founder’s purposes or established usage. A mere apprehension that regulatory powers may be abused does not invalidate the provision.

predicates.challenge_to_religious_trust_regulation: The litigants challenged a law providing oversight of religious trusts.
predicates.oversight_is_limited_to_proper_trust_adm: The regulator’s powers are confined to proper administration of the trust under its governing law and purposes.
predicates.religious_practices_are_not_interfered_w: The oversight does not interfere with practices regarded by the religious community as part of its religion.
predicates.trust_funds_remain_directed_to_authorize: The oversight does not divert trust property or income from purposes established by the founder or by established usage.

issues.definition: If trust oversight is confined to proper administration, does not interfere with religious practices, and leaves trust funds directed to authorized purposes, it does not unconstitutionally infringe religious freedom or religious affairs.

issues.legal_issue: A contribution imposed on religious trusts to meet the expenses of administering a regulatory scheme is a fee rather than a tax when it funds that administration rather than general public revenue or the promotion of a religion.
material_facts: The legislation required trustees to pay a contribution, subject to a limit, for expenses incurred or to be incurred in administering the regulatory scheme.
The contribution was imposed to support the administration of religious trusts and was not for promoting or maintaining a particular religion or denomination.
issues.conclusion: The contribution was a valid fee, not an unauthorized tax, and did not violate the constitutional prohibition on appropriating tax proceeds for the promotion or maintenance of a religion.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the distinction between a tax and a fee and relied on Mahant Shri Jagannath Ramanuj Das v. The State of Orissa, [1954] S.C.R. 1046, which upheld an analogous contribution for the administration of religious endowments. Article 27 prohibits specific appropriation of tax proceeds to promote or maintain a particular religion or religious denomination; it did not apply to a fee for secular administration of religious institutions.

predicates.challenge_to_religious_trust_administrat: The litigants challenged a charge imposed on religious trusts in connection with administration of a regulatory scheme.
predicates.charge_funds_administration_of_trust_reg: The charge was collected to meet the expenses of administering the trust-regulation scheme.
predicates.charge_is_not_appropriated_to_promote_a_: The charge was not specifically appropriated to promote or maintain a particular religion or denomination.

issues.definition: A charge challenged in trust-regulation proceedings is a valid administrative fee rather than a prohibited tax when it funds administration and is not appropriated to promote a religion.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory restriction on further appeals does not displace the constitutional jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to hear an appeal when the constitutional requirements for that appeal are met.
material_facts: The legislation provided for an appeal to the High Court from an order of a District Judge and stated that no appeal would lie from an order made in appeal under that provision.
The appellants argued that the restriction contravened the constitutional provision governing appeals to the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The restriction did not override the constitutional provisions governing appeals to the Supreme Court and did not affect the Court’s jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: The Court interpreted the statutory appeal restriction as not overriding Article 133 or any other constitutional provision governing appeals to the Supreme Court. A statute cannot affect the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction where the constitutional requirements for an appeal are fulfilled.

predicates.challenge_to_statutory_appeal_restrictio: A litigant challenged a statutory provision limiting further appeals from an appellate order.
predicates.statute_limits_further_ordinary_appeals: The statute restricted further appeals within the ordinary statutory appeal process.
predicates.constitutional_appeal_requirements_are_s: The requirements imposed by the Constitution for an appeal to the Supreme Court are fulfilled.

issues.definition: When a statute limits further ordinary appeals but the constitutional requirements for a Supreme Court appeal are satisfied, Supreme Court appeal jurisdiction remains available.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a religious institution or its property is private or public cannot be determined in writ proceedings when the issue requires investigation of complicated facts and evidence that is not available on the record.
material_facts: The appellants asserted that some institutions or properties were private, while the State disputed those assertions and claimed that the institutions were public religious trusts.
The competing claims about the nature of the institutions and properties required investigation of complicated facts and the recording of evidence.

The record did not contain material enabling the Court to determine the nature of the trusts; in one proceeding, the proposed amendment to plead a private character was refused because it would alter the character of the suit.
issues.conclusion: The nature of the trusts and properties could not be determined on the record in these proceedings; the appeals were decided on the constitutional validity of the legislation instead.
issues.legal_principle: The Court agreed that questions whether a trust is public or private, and whether property is private or trust property, may require factual investigation and evidence and therefore could not be resolved on the writ record in these cases. No earlier case was relied on for this procedural conclusion.

predicates.writ_proceeding: The claim about the trust’s status is raised in a writ proceeding.
predicates.competing_claims_concern_public_or_priva: The parties dispute whether the religious institution or its property is public or private.
predicates.resolution_requires_complex_factual_inve: Resolving the dispute requires investigation of complicated facts and the recording of evidence.
predicates.evidentiary_record_is_inadequate: The record in the proceeding does not contain sufficient evidence to resolve the dispute.

issues.definition: When a writ proceeding presents a disputed public-or-private trust status that requires complex factual investigation and the record is inadequate, that status cannot be determined in the writ proceeding.
